text: When an order gives a target spot off to one side of a belt, don't assume that side is free to build on: check the area, and if you can't tell, build compactly right next to the belt and say in chat which side you chose so the player can correct it early. Also, an area scan with a small radius can cut a belt line off; look around the reported end before treating it as the real end.

When powering a remote spot, run the power step from the nearest pole already wired to the real grid (or the original grid pole), not from a pole you just placed. Then check the new poles joined that grid instead of forming an isolated island. Bridge any gap longer than the small pole's 7.5-tile wire reach with an extra pole.

A fresh production build measures 0 per minute until its buffers fill and the first crafts finish, so the first plan should end with a wait step (60-120 s) before checking. Its expect checks should look at what's in the output chest and which machines are working, not the rate measured right after building.

For a "N per minute into a chest" order, the rate is judged by how fast the chest count grows, so never take finished products back out of the output chest and keep its contents out of the fetchable supply. The plan should end with a long wait (2+ minutes) so the rate can be measured in steady state.

When an order says "into a chest" at a rate, put one output chest compactly close to the spots the order points at (within ~15-20 tiles), not at the far end of a long build, because the rate checker may only look for chests near the order location. Keep the build compact around the given belts instead of extending them far away.

For long-distance outposts (>~200 tiles), split belt connects and power runs into legs of under ~150 tiles via waypoints, and check that the first new pole is within wire reach of the existing grid pole (add a bridging pole if needed). Expect checks on far-away delivery need a wait step long enough for items to travel the belt (~1.9 tiles/s on yellow belt), and drill 'working' checks shouldn't use

When a player keeps reporting a rate as 0 while production stats show it's working, the checker is watching a different spot. Don't just wait and re-verify: move the output chest right next to the order's given input belts or spots, and feed every producer into that one chest.

When the order text repeats earlier "not done yet" lines, check the actual state first (find the item and diagnose its rate) before rebuilding, because those lines are often old history rather than fresh failures. If the build is verifiably working, submit a short wait with expect checks on the output chest that the order is judged by.

When you move a build's output to a new chest, empty and remove the old output chest right away, because a stale chest still holding product can be what a checker reads, and then the rate shows as 0. Keep exactly one output chest for the product.

If a player's rate check keeps saying 0 after one fix while game stats show production, stop guessing at relayouts. Ask in chat which chest or stat they measure, and keep the original output chest in place in the meantime, because a checker may be tracking that specific chest.

When an order says to automate something from given belts, don't put buffer chests inside the production chain. Pass intermediates by direct insertion or on belts (a single belt tile works as a buffer), and keep the only chest at the final output, because chests mid-chain can count as hand-feeding.

Before building a production expansion, check the power grid's boiler fuel supply (and refuel/automate it first) and check that the existing output belt has a sink, since a dead grid or a backed-up output makes every new machine idle. Don't add take steps for scattered raw materials listed by find (counts change fast); just craft what's needed and let the actor fetch it.

When a single belt feeds a row of several machines, size the feed for all of them: one basic inserter loading from a chest gives under 1 plate/s, and the first machine eats it all, so use several loading inserters (or a real plate belt). Also cap each output chest with a slot limit, so upstream machines stop once full and the input reaches the machines further down.

When scaling production, plan ~15% more ore than the target (some drills sit on thin ore and deplete) and check fuel for every burner in the chain, including existing hand-fed furnaces and boilers, topping them up in the same plan. Never add a craft step for items the character already carries; just place them.

Before chaining block/route/merge steps, look up the real port tiles (block_info and an area look at the actual belt ends after each build), and never send a route or connect line through a tile that a later merge_lanes needs. Feed a two-item block input from two pure lines that side-load opposite sides of one straight belt, never two lines onto the same side. Bootstrap scarce ingredients first (e

A production order is only as durable as its fuel: in the first plan, give every burner in the chain (boilers, old and new furnaces) an automatic coal feed sized for the doubled load (boiler chests with inserters at minimum, ideally a coal belt), because hand-loaded fuel runs out between checks and the rate collapses. Chests used as fuel buffers get raided by fetch steps, so refill them last and k

For a multi-part build, submit every part in sequence with more=true and never resubmit an earlier part while later ones are queued (a new submit replaces the running plan and silently drops the queued parts); before chaining blocks, check that each block's input belt really ends at the block (a belt running one tile past it can side-load raw plates into a neighbouring route) and remove an existin

Never add coal to an ore belt with a lone inserter or side-load unless you've confirmed which lane the drills fill: coal must sit on its own lane or it backs up the ore lane and jams the smelters. Also don't resubmit a non-"more" plan while earlier parts are still queued, because it cancels them; get the raw supply working (plates flowing, every burner fuelled) before building the science blocks d

When connecting a block's output belt, never start or route it on a tile directly in front of the end of any other belt (including the block's own internal belts), and join a shared belt only by a true side-load onto the empty lane (check which lane existing items ride and where the line turns before choosing the side). To combine two pure belt lines into one two-lane belt, lay every tile yourself with a ghosts step: each feeder's last tile points sideways into the merged belt from opposite sides, and the merged belt runs far enough downstream for the row that follows. Don't rely on connect plus merge_lanes, because connect can route into the merge tile and the checker rejects later steps on belts that don't exis

For any sustained production order, supply every raw input from mining and smelting in the first plan, never from a stock of plates in chests. A chest-fed ingredient (e.g. iron for gears) runs dry within minutes, and the rate check then fails at a fraction of the target. Size each ingredient's supply to the full target rate plus margin, and check that every machine in the line is fed, not just the

When wiring a new build to a given grid pole, put your own pole within wire reach of it as an explicit ghost (medium pole within ~7 tiles of the grid pole, next to the build's nearest pole), and don't rely on a power step's "from". That step can route a small-pole line just out of reach and leave the build as an unpowered island.

When a long power line ends at an outpost, place the outpost's own poles as part of that same pole line, spaced within wire reach of its last pole, then check they're on the grid; poles placed before the line arrives can stay a separate unpowered island even when they're close. For a delivery over 200+ tiles, the final wait must cover the belt travel time after the drills get power (distance/1.9 s

A single connect over ~100+ tiles can fail with "no route found within search limit", so split any long belt run into legs of about 50-60 tiles through waypoints on open ground from the start. Put the legs in their own part before the builds that depend on them, because a failed step drops every queued part after it.

Before adding electric load, inspect the boilers' fuel feed itself: an electric inserter feeding a boiler deadlocks once coal runs out, so replace it with a burner inserter plus a big coal chest for every boiler in the first plan. Also make sure every furnace column's output belt ends in a sink (inserters into chests), because a backed-up output caps the plate rate no matter how many furnaces you

Only add refuel steps for burners you've confirmed by name at that tile (an area entry saying boiler, not a steam engine or "grid low on fuel"), or leave boiler fuel to the actor, which tops grids up itself. When a mall belt feeds plates and an intermediate made at its head, make sure the plate feed gets its own large stock and its own fast inserter, and check that the belt carries plates (belt_ca

Before placing electric drills on an ore patch, pick the drill spots from find's per-tile ore list (dense tiles covering the whole 3x3 footprint, clear of trees and old burner drills) rather than the patch's bounding box. In that same first plan, check the grid's boilers: refuel them and make their feed a burner inserter from a coal chest, because an electric boiler inserter deadlocks once power d

For a mall or any lasting build, first look for an existing plate belt or smelter line (including backed-up furnaces whose belt stops just short of a join) and feed the build from it with a splitter, because hand-stocked feed chests drain within minutes and every rate check then fails. Size intermediate feeds to their consumers: give a shared intermediate (gears) its own fast inserter onto the bel

When an intermediate maker (gears) feeds both a product chest and a shared belt, cap the chest with a 1-slot limit and size the maker (assembling-machine-2, fast output inserter) for every consumer's rate from the first plan. For raw inputs that only come from trees (wood), first find a real tree cluster and gather 100+ in one trip, then stock it; don't clear spots without confirmed trees or inser

When one plate belt feeds several buffer chests in series, the first inserter hogs the plates, so cap each buffer chest with a 1-slot limit from the start and put the bottleneck intermediate maker (gears) first on the line. Before declaring a mall done, diagnose the shared intermediate's supply against the sum of every consumer's target rate.

For long pole runs to a remote outpost, use connect with small-electric-pole in legs of about 50-70 tiles through waypoints, not the power step, which can crash on long remote runs. Put the remote machine (e.g. a pumpjack for a trigger tech) after the pole legs so it's powered as soon as it's placed.

To keep N labs busy, size science supply to the labs' consumption: one assembling-machine-1 on red science makes only about 6 packs/min, enough for roughly one lab, so plan at least one red-science assembler per lab (more for fast techs), each inserting straight into a lab. Lab-to-lab inserters only share packs; they don't add any.

Before building on an existing oil/chemical setup, verify every fluid consumer actually runs: check which inlet gets which fluid and whether one plant hogs a shared petroleum line because its output never backs up. Give each product (e.g. sulfur vs plastic) its own output belt or lane that can back up, and feed burner-style ingredients like coal by belt instead of a hand-filled chest.

When an outpost cluster (e.g. coal drills) sits more than ~7 tiles from your nearest planned pole, put an explicit bridging pole in the ghosts so every gap between poles is at most 7 tiles (check the diagonal distance, not just dx or dy). A power step to a far spot can leave its new poles just out of reach as a dead island.

When feeding a two-lane block input from two separate lines, lay both final side-load tiles yourself with ghosts from opposite sides of the merge belt (never rely on connect's end_direction, which can arrive from the wrong side and put both items on one lane, where the backed-up one blocks the other forever). Before building on an existing plate supply, diagnose that plate first and give every bur

If a production build adds electric load to a grid whose boiler is hand-fed, the first plan must also give that boiler a coal belt from electric drills on a coal patch, ending at a burner inserter. Size it at about 2x the boiler's burn, even if the belt is long (lay it in 50-60 tile legs). A hand-filled boiler dies within minutes, and every machine on the grid stops with it.

For a rate target, build about 20% more producers than the exact math (e.g. 6 red science assemblers for 30/min, not 5). Size every input to match, because a build running at exactly the target rate can still read as "not done" in the rate check.

Before placing new machines next to existing ones, scan the whole footprint with a small-radius area look and check it against every belt line's route, because long connect-built belts snake through crowded spots that a wider scan only reports by their ends. When space is tight, put new machines on tiles freed by removing obsolete hand-fed machines rather than on open-looking spots.

When placing poles by hand in a ghosts layout, check every inserter and machine against each pole's actual supply square (medium pole covers only the 7x7 tiles centered on it, i.e. ±3 tiles; small pole 5x5), not just the wire chain. Inserters in gaps between assemblers and in the rows above/below them are the ones most often left one tile outside coverage, so add a pole beside each such inserter r

When a rate order's check counts the product in the output chest, plan the final wait to cover start-up plus enough steady output for a full count (e.g. 3+ minutes at 5-10/min), and build about 50% more of the final assembler than the exact math, since one machine barely over target reads as short. Don't use a "working" check with recipe=<ore> for mining drills (drills have no recipe, so it finds none). Check drills with "powered" near them plus "belt_carries" of the ore at the delivery belt end, and when an order says to power from a specific grid, link that grid's pole to the build's pole line in the first plan.

Wood is not a minable resource name: to get wood, use a clear step with trees=true on a confirmed tree cluster from find "tree", then insert the wood without a fixed count. Gather the wood before the plan's later steps need it (e.g. for small-electric-pole recipes).

Before scaling up production, follow the existing output belt to its real end and check that something takes from it. A dead-end tile or a backed-up belt with full furnaces means the existing line is stalled and the doubled rate will fall short. In the first plan, give every line (old and new) a working sink, such as a fixed belt join or inserters into chests at the belt end.

When a place step is blocked by a character, it's often another player standing still, so moving serf won't clear it; re-plan that entity onto a different free tile or side of the machine. When laying small feeds beside machines in a busy spot, give each input a fallback side so one blocked tile doesn't stall the plan.

When a chemical plant reports its fluid inlets swapped, don't rotate or re-place it, because direction changes don't move its inlets here. Instead swap the feeds at the inlet tiles: take out the two inlet pipes and bring one fluid in with a pipe-to-ground pair under the other line, leaving no new pipe touching the other fluid. Before building a new consumer on an existing plate belt, trace that belt back to its furnaces and check that they're fuelled by belt or inserter rather than by hand. If any furnace or drill feeding it runs on hand-loaded coal, give it a belt-fed coal lane (ore and coal on separate lanes) in the same first plan.

Before building anything, look at the grid's boiler: if it's hand-fed, first stock it with hundreds of coal through a burner inserter and chest, because a dead grid makes every later power step fail with "no powered pole".
